Now, regarding the second part of your question, a step function f / [a, b] -> \mathbb{R} is Riemann Integrable if and only if it is bounded and has at most a countable number of discontinuities.

To prove this, we can use the following steps:

1. Let f be a step function on [a, b]. Then, there exists a partition P of [a, b] such that f is constant on each subinterval [x_i, x_{i+1}].
2. Since f is constant on each subinterval, it is bounded on each subinterval.
3. Since f is bounded on each subinterval, it is bounded on [a, b].
4. Let {x_n} be a sequence of points in [a, b] such that f(x_n) is discontinuous. Then, there exists an open interval (x_n, x_{n+1}) such that f is not constant on (x_n, x_{n+1}).
5. Since f is constant on each subinterval [x_i, x_{i+1}], it is constant on (x_n, x_{n+1}). Therefore, f(x_n) = f(x_{n+1}).
6. This implies that f(x_n) is not discontinuous at x_n.
7. Since there are only countably many points in [a, b], there are only countably many points {x_n} such that f(x_n) is discontinuous.
8. Therefore, f has at most a countable number of discontinuities.
9. Since f is bounded and has at most a countable number of discontinuities, it is Riemann Integrable.

Note that this proof assumes that the step function f is defined on a closed interval [a, b]. If f is defined on an open interval (a, b), then the proof is similar, but with the partition P being a finite collection of points in (a, b) instead of a finite collection of points in [a, b].
